Sighing
SY-ing
n. and v. (pres. part.)
From sigh, Saxon sican, to draw a long breath. Webster 1828: the act of sighing; a deep and audible respiration expressing grief or longing. It is grief too deep or too tired for words, and Scripture treats it as prayer God hears.

Biblical Definition

Sighing is inarticulate grief, and the remarkable thing in Scripture is that God answers it as though it were speech. For the oppression of the poor, for the sighing of the needy, now will I arise, saith the LORD; I will set him in safety from him that puffeth at him (Psalm 12:5). No petition is recorded, no argument is made; there is only sighing, and God says now will I arise. The psalmist elsewhere describes his own life measured out in it: For my life is spent with grief, and my years with sighing: my strength faileth because of mine iniquity, and my bones are consumed (Psalm 31:10) — and he traces the cause honestly to his own sin, not to circumstance. God can also silence sighing in judgment, which is a terrible thing to read: Go up, O Elam: besiege, O Media; all the sighing thereof have I made to cease (Isaiah 21:2), spoken of Babylon, whose oppression of others is being ended by ending Babylon. And the word receives its final answer in one of the great promises: And the ransomed of the LORD shall return, and come to Zion with songs and everlasting joy upon their heads: they shall obtain joy and gladness, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away (Isaiah 35:10).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SIGHING as the act of sighing — a deep, long, and audible respiration or single inspiration, occasioned by grief, oppression of the heart, or earnest longing.

expand to see more

SIGHING, n. — The act of sighing; a deep and audible respiration expressing grief, weariness, or longing.

SIGH, v.i. — To inhale a larger quantity of air than usual and emit it audibly, as under the pressure of sorrow.

Figuratively, to lament; to mourn; to express grief without words.

In Scripture, often joined with groaning and with crying, as the sound of an oppressed people.

From Saxon sican, to sigh — probably imitative of the sound of the breath.

Key Scripture

Psalm 12:5 — "For the oppression of the poor, for the sighing of the needy, now will I arise, saith the LORD; I will set him in safety from him that puffeth at him."

Psalm 31:10 — "For my life is spent with grief, and my years with sighing: my strength faileth because of mine iniquity, and my bones are consumed."

Isaiah 21:2 — "A grievous vision is declared unto me; the treacherous dealer dealeth treacherously, and the spoiler spoileth. Go up, O Elam: besiege, O Media; all the sighing thereof have I made to cease."

Isaiah 35:10 — "And the ransomed of the LORD shall return, and come to Zion with songs and everlasting joy upon their heads: they shall obtain joy and gladness, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away."

Modern Corruption

Psalm 12:5 has God arising for the sighing of the needy, and both the prosperity teaching that a sighing believer lacks faith and the religious sentimentality that treats such promises as merely inward comfort miss what the verse says God will do.

expand to see more

The verse is a divine oath in the middle of a psalm about flattering lips and the vanishing of the godly, and its structure is worth attending to. The cause is the oppression of the poor and the sighing of the needy; the response is now will I arise, saith the LORD; the outcome is I will set him in safety from him that puffeth at him. No repentance is required of the needy first, no eloquence, no formula. Against the teaching that a believer’s difficulty is evidence of insufficient faith or a negative confession, this psalm has God moved by a sound made by people with nothing left to say. Romans 8:26 continues the pattern into the New Testament: the Spirit makes intercession with groanings which cannot be uttered.

The second corruption reduces the promise to a feeling. Psalm 12:5 says God will set him in safety, and Isaiah 35:10 says the ransomed will come to Zion with everlasting joy on their heads and that sorrow and sighing shall flee away. These are promises of an actual state of affairs, secured by an actual redemption, and consummated in a real new heaven and new earth where God shall wipe away all tears (Revelation 21:4). Read as inward consolation only, they are thin. Read as what they say, they are the ground on which a believer may sigh without pretence and still hope without embarrassment. Psalm 31:10 shows the honest form of it: the psalmist names his own iniquity as the cause and sighs anyway, to the God he has offended.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew anachah (H585), a sighing, a groaning; anach (H584), to sigh, to groan; naaqah (H5009), a groaning; Greek stenazo (G4727), to groan, to sigh inwardly.

expand to see more

Hebrew anachah (H585) — a sigh, a groan; sorrow and sighing shall flee away (Isaiah 35:10).

Hebrew anach (H584) — to sigh, to groan; the verb behind the sighing of the oppressed.

Hebrew naaqah (H5009) — a groaning; I have heard the groaning of the children of Israel (Exodus 6:5).

Greek stenazo (G4727) — to groan inwardly; we that are in this tabernacle do groan, being burdened (2 Corinthians 5:4).

Greek stenagmos (G4726) — a groaning; the unutterable groanings of the Spirit in Romans 8:26.

Usage

"For the sighing of the needy, now will I arise, saith the LORD (Psalm 12:5) — God answering a sound, not an argument."

"My years with sighing… because of mine iniquity (Psalm 31:10) — grief honestly traced to its cause."

"Sorrow and sighing shall flee away (Isaiah 35:10) — the promised end of the sound."
